points: Shuffling a column's values and re-scoring the model shows how much it depends on that column. The largest effects: 'x1' (9.722, 67% of the total); 'cat' (3.067, 21% of the total); 'x2' (1.82, 12% of the total); 'when' (-0.017, 0% of the total).

The model's own internal weights agree: 'x1' is also its heaviest input (45%). Two different views pointing the same way make this a sturdier finding.

permutation.note: Importance describes what the model uses to predict. It does not show that a column causes the outcome, and correlated columns can share importance between them.
permutation.reading: Importance is the drop in the score when a column's values are shuffled; a drop near zero means the model barely uses that column. 'reliable' means the drop is more than twice its run-to-run variation.

shap.reason: SHAP is not part of this build, so no SHAP values are computed or claimed. Permutation importance, partial dependence and one-column-at-a-time local effects are provided instead.

limitations: The model describes patterns in the data it was trained on. It does not show what causes the outcome, and it can be wrong for new situations that differ from the training data.
Scores come from one random split plus cross-validation; with different data or a different seed they will move by a normal amount.
A prediction is a single best estimate. The typical-error range comes from held-out rows and does not bound any individual prediction.

metrics_plan.note: Scores are ranked so that higher is always better (error metrics are shown with their sign flipped inside the ranking and as ordinary positive numbers in tables).
reasons: Models are ranked by RMSE, which is in the units of the target and penalises large misses.

problem.why: The target is numeric with many distinct values, so the task is to predict a number (regression).

reproducibility.statement: The same dataset version, configuration and seed reproduce the same split, folds and model on the same library versions.

validation.selection_rule: Models are ranked by their mean cross-validation score on the training rows. The held-out test rows are used only to report each model's final score, never to choose among models.
